name: components
// release: No `manifestRootsToUpdate`: the package is produced AFTER the version bump (tools/release.mjs), so dist carries the right version from the build itself. Patching the manifest in dist was needed only in the reverse order — and it was a half-measure, because it fixed one file and not the constant compiled into the bundle.
// implicitDependencies: The package carries the skin generated by `tokens` but imports nothing from it in TS — without this entry the graph does not know that edge and the build starts before the CSS is generated.
// themes: ng-packagr does not read assets from outside the project directory, so the skin has to become an input of the package first. `themes/` is generated and gitignored — the only source of truth remains the DTCG files in libs/tokens/src.
// schematics: Compiled separately and AFTER ng-packagr, because ng-packagr cleans dist on start — a schematics build wired in earlier would be deleted. The migration collection is in the package from the first release deliberately: `ng update` reads it from the INSTALLED version, so adding it only at the first breaking change would help nobody who installed earlier. The last copy (`package.dist.json` → `schematics/package.json`) closes the module boundary: the package manifest carries `"type": "module"` from ng-packagr while these files are CommonJS (`exports.ngAdd = …`), so without a `{ "type": "commonjs" }` of their own Node reads them as ESM and `ng add @pacit/components` ends in `exports is not defined in ES module scope` — at the consumer's, on the first command they type. `check-package` does not see this by design: it asks whether the factory file EXISTS, not whether it can be loaded. The file is called `package.dist.json` rather than `package.json`, because a real manifest in the repository tree IS a project to Nx (`lesson-44`). `@angular/cdk` solves it the same way. It depends on `citations` as well as on `build`, and the order is load-bearing: `build` owns the whole of `dist/libs/components` and a cached restore of it re-materialises the directory, so a step writing inside it has to stand after `build` in ONE graph — two `nx` invocations restore `build` twice and the second wipes the first's work (measured 2026-09-17: `schematics/` gone after `citations` ran on its own).
// test: The `coverageInclude` patterns run from the repository root, not from the project directory — whatever the executor schema says: the `**/src/**` version pulled the whole of `apps/sandbox` into the library's report. Templates stand there beside the code, because `@if`/`@for` logic is code, and without this entry they drop out of the report entirely. The reasons for the `coverageExclude` exceptions are held by `tools/check-coverage.mjs` (the `SKIPPED` constant) — that is what decides what the gate REQUIRES in the report, and this list has to be a subset of it: were it to exclude anything more, the file would drop out of the report and fire point 3. `coverageThresholds` declares BOTH numbers, the lines and the branches: vitest enforces the keys it is handed and infers none, so `lines` alone leaves every condition in the library under no floor at all. Neither of the two reaches a template — 47 of the 535 branches and 136 of the 694 lines are template ones, so any single template can go unrendered without moving either total off its threshold. That is what point 6 of the gate is for.
// check-coverage: The sources are in `inputs` OUTRIGHT, even though the report comes from `test`: a file v8 cannot count changes the report by not one byte, so `dependentTasksOutputFiles` alone would give a cache hit and the gate would not fire on the one thing it was built for. The comments stand HERE rather than in the target: the executor's `options` has `additionalProperties: false`, and a `// …` key inside `targets` breaks the graph (`lesson-43`). The templates stand in `inputs` beside the sources for that same reason: point 6 holds each of them to a floor of its own, so a changed `@if` has to invalidate the cache even when not one `.ts` moved.
// check-zoneless: The sources are in `inputs` OUTRIGHT, beside the build output, because points 4 and 6 read them DIRECTLY — and a cache key is to list what the gate reads, not what usually changes along with it. Measured: an explicit `standalone: true` in the decorator leaves `ɵɵngDeclareComponent` unchanged (the declaration carries `isStandalone: true` anyway) and moves `ɵɵngDeclareClassMetadata` alone, that is the decorator's echo for debugging. The cache would therefore be invalidated today even without this entry — but through a diagnostic feature that is nobody's promise. The day ng-packagr stops emitting it would be the day point 6 quietly stops firing (`lesson-44` in its third disguise). The `**/package.json` pattern covers the manifests of every project, including one yet to exist: the gate reads them from the git index, so a list hard-coded here would drift with the first new library.
// check-files: The file-structure gate: the fixed layout of an entrypoint, and the template and the stylesheet of every component in files of their own (decision 0001). It stands in `components` rather than in the root project for `check-styles`'s reason — everything it reads lies in the library — and it depends on no build: the promise is about the SOURCE TREE, so an artefact would be one transformation too many between the rule and what it rules on. `inputs` name the four kinds of material the gate reads and nothing else: the TS sources (the declarations, and the specs point 3 asks about), the templates and stylesheets (the file list points 6 and 7 compare in both directions), the entrypoint manifests (the denominator of points 2, 3 and 8) and `files.policy.json` (the register points 4, 5 and 9 read). The patterns are global within the project rather than a list of names, for the reason written under `check-styles`: a new entrypoint is to be covered from its first commit, and a hard-coded list would drift at the first one. There are no `externalDependencies` — the gate is hand-written and its only outside reader is `git ls-files`, which is how it asks what the repository really carries rather than what happens to be lying on the disk.
// check-styles: The stylesheet gate: logical properties, no compositing `opacity`, no rule of forced-colors mode outranked by a base rule of the same sheet, no property that paints the inside of an icon, and no duration a component timed itself instead of taking from the motion axis. It does not depend on `build` — it reads the SOURCES, because only they carry the exception markers and only they have line numbers to navigate somebody by. The sass output is produced inside the gate, from those same files. `inputs` list the stylesheets (the material), the TS sources (the denominator of point 3 — a component styling itself outside a stylesheet), the DTCG token sources and the e2e specs (the two sides of point 10 — which custom property carries the touch floor, and which floor is measured in a browser), and the fixtures. The last two belong to other projects on purpose: `req-a11y-touch` is one promise spread over three trees, and a gate that could see only the sheets is how it came to have two disagreeing lists (`lesson-194`) — so a token re-pointed away from `{pct.target.min}`, or a measurement deleted from `target-min.spec.ts`, has to invalidate this cache rather than be answered from a run taken before it. The patterns are global within the project rather than a list of names: a new entrypoint is to be covered from its first commit, and a hard-coded list would drift at the first one — and then it would be the gate that stopped seeing, not CI that fired.
// check-bundle: The tree-shaking and size-budget gate. It stands in `components` rather than in the root project, because everything it reads lies in the library and in its `dist` — and a new entrypoint is a change in `libs/components`, so it makes this project affected from its first commit. `inputs` list the entrypoint manifests (the list the measurement walks), the snapshot (the other side of the comparison), the script and the fixtures. `dependsOn` on `build` is hard: the gate bundles the ARTEFACT, not the sources, because the artefact is what a consumer gets — the probes reach for the package through `node_modules` and the `exports` map, the same road they take. `externalDependencies` list esbuild (the fast probes), `@babel/core` with `@angular/compiler-cli` (the linker the probes run over the package, so that the number is what an application carries rather than what the tarball weighs) plus `@angular/build` and `@angular/cli` (the probe with the real builder): bumping any of them changes the measured sizes, so it has to invalidate the cache — otherwise the budget would guard a number from before the bump.
// check-consumer: The consumer gate: it reproduces the whole road from `npm pack` through a local registry to a button painted by a token in the browser. It stands in `components`, because it measures THIS package. `dependsOn` on `build` and `schematics` is hard — it packs the artefact together with the `ng add` collection, and without that point 4 has nothing to run. `inputs` list the output of both targets, the Verdaccio configuration (the gate publishes through it rather than through a copy of its own), the script and the fixtures. `externalDependencies` are long because the road is long: bumping Verdaccio changes the registry, bumping `@angular/cli`/`@angular/build`/`@angular/ssr`/`@angular/router` changes the build and server-side rendering, `express` carries the application server, and `@playwright/test` is the browser — each of them can change the RESULT of the measurement with the package unchanged, so each has to invalidate the cache. The gate does not install `peerDependencies` from the registry: the application takes `@angular/*` from the repository's `node_modules` by searching up the tree, just as the builder probe in `check-bundle` does. The price is written down plainly — a version-range drift in `peerDependencies` passes this gate, and only `req-project-dependencies` watches for it.
// check-texts: The text-channel gate: it watches that a string the library writes goes through `PCT_TEXTS`. It stands in `components`, because everything it reads lies in the library and in its `dist`. `dependsOn` on `build` is hard: point 2 compares the read from the sources with `ɵcmp.consts` and `ɵdir.hostAttrs` after linking, that is with the output of the real compiler — without that an attribute brought in by an object spread inside a `host` block (`...fitHost` in `field/src/affix.ts`) would have no way of showing up. `inputs` list the templates and the sources OUTRIGHT, beside the build output: the gate reads them directly, and a cache key is to list what it reads rather than what usually changes along with it (`lesson-44`). `externalDependencies` list `@angular/compiler`, because its `parseTemplate` and `TmplAstRecursiveVisitor` are what read the template — an Angular bump may add a node kind the walk does not know, and that is to invalidate the cache rather than pass unnoticed.
// check-harness: The harness gate: one harness per component in `@pacit/components/testing`, and each one a declaration held to the package in both directions — the host selector to the class's own, the parts to what the class draws, the declared union to the list, the cards' rows to the names. It stands in `components` for `check-bundle`'s reason: everything it reads lies in the library, its `dist` and the cards. `dependsOn` on `build` is hard — the gate reads `ɵcmp` after linking and the emitted declaration file, so a harness written against a source nobody built is exactly what it must not trust. `inputs` list the build output, the cards (point 6 reads their Harness rows), the script and the fixtures; `@angular/cdk` is an external dependency because the base class is the CDK's, and a CDK bump that changes what a harness is has to invalidate the cache.
// mutation: Stryker's mutation run on the core (`core`, `[pctNumber]`, `PctSelect`) — the only machine that answers whether the unit tests catch anything (`req-quality-unit`). It does not depend on `build`: it mutates the SOURCES and runs them with a Vitest configuration of its own (`mutation.vitest.config.mts`), because the `test` target goes through the `@angular/build` builder, which has no configuration file and cannot have one — it assembles it in memory. `inputs` list the sources and specs of the WHOLE library, not of the mutated files alone: a `select.ts` mutant is sometimes killed by a test in `field.spec.ts`, so a change to any spec can change the result. `externalDependencies` list Stryker with its runner, Vitest and the Analog plugin: bumping any of them changes the set of mutants or the way they are run, so it has to invalidate the cache — otherwise the threshold would guard a number from before the bump. The target itself fails below `thresholds.break`; WHY that is not enough is explained by `check-mutation`.
// check-mutation: The gate over the mutation run. Stryker can fire by itself and by default does NOT — `thresholds.break` is `null` by definition, so the run ends with zero whatever the score. And once a threshold does stand, it is raised by five moves, none of which adds a test: a file struck out of `mutate`, widened `ignorers` or a `// Stryker disable` in the source, an excluded mutator family, `ignoreStatic: true`, a shortened `timeoutMS` (a mutant killed by the CLOCK counts as killed by an assertion). The gate reads the EFFECTIVE configuration from the report, not from the file — `--ignoreStatic` in the target's command leaves no trace in it. `inputs` take the output of `mutation`, the policy, the snapshot, the Stryker configuration, `project.json` (the target's command) and the workflow (point 7).
// typecheck: Four runs, because the library has four disjoint programs: the package (`tsconfig.lib.json`), the specs together with `testing/` (`tsconfig.spec.json`), the mutation run's configuration (`tsconfig.mutation.json`) and the schematics compiled to CommonJS (`schematics/tsconfig.json`). They overlap in one file and one direction only: `tsconfig.spec.json` took `schematics/**/*.spec.ts` when the first migration shipped with cases, and a spec that imports the migration pulls its source into the spec program as well as the schematics one — the reverse does not happen, because `schematics/tsconfig.json` excludes specs and emits none. Otherwise none of them sees the files of the others, so one invocation would check part of the library and look like the whole — it is `check-typecheck` that compares this sum against the file list from the git index. `inputs` take `default` and NOT `production`: `production` subtracts `**/*.spec.ts`. Measured, not assumed — adding a line to `src/public-api.spec.ts` gives `Cache: 0/1 hit` with `default` and `1/1 hit` with `production`, that is the second run does NOT move exactly when it is needed (`lesson-44` in another disguise). `build` checks types along the way, but for `tsconfig.lib.prod.json` alone — the rest have no compiler other than this target.
// stamp-version: Copies `version` from the manifest into the PCT_VERSION constant. Deliberately NOT a dependency of `build`: were the build to stamp itself, the artefact would always agree and the `check-package` gate would stop examining anything. It is run by the release (after the version bump) and by a person — and the gate watches that nobody forgot.
// citations: Rewrites the citations the JSDoc carries — repository paths and bare `req-*` / `lesson-*` identifiers — onto the documentation site, the origin read from `apps/docs/public/CNAME` (decision 0078). A step after `build` and not part of it, with its own outputs inside the package: `check-package` point 9 then reads the artefact for what it missed, which is the same relationship `stamp-version` has with point 4.
